title: Counting and averaging
objectives: Use `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` on a whole table
Predict how many rows an aggregate query returns

screens.title: One value from many rows
screens.prose:
The `prices` table holds a week of AstraZeneca closes, one row per trading day. This query asks it a question about the whole week.

```sql
SELECT MAX(close)
FROM prices;
```

state.caption: prices: one row per trading day

screens.question: Tap the value this query returns.

hints.text: `MAX` keeps one value from the column it is given.
The query reads only the close column.
Compare the five closes and keep the largest.

feedback.correct: `MAX(close)` read all five closes and kept the largest, £120.25.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look down the whole close column for its largest value.

byKey.r4c2: You picked the latest close. `MAX` compares every row, not just the last one.
byKey.r0c2: You picked the first row. `MAX` looks at every close before it answers.
byKey.r2c2: That is the smallest close. `MIN(close)` would return it.

explain.text: You scanned the whole close column and kept one number. `MAX` does exactly that, and so do `MIN`, `SUM`, `AVG` and `COUNT` in their own ways.

screens.title: Which rows take part
screens.prose:
This query adds up a column.

```sql
SELECT SUM(volume)
FROM prices;
```
screens.question: Tap every volume that `SUM(volume)` adds.

hints.text: Is there anything in the query that leaves a row out?
There is no `WHERE` line.
Every row feeds the sum, so tap all five volumes.

feedback.correct: All five rows feed the sum: 10,600,000 shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Nothing in this query leaves a row out.

explain.text: With no `WHERE`, every row feeds the aggregate. The five volumes add to 10,600,000 shares, returned as one value.

screens.title: The shape of the answer
screens.prose:
Now we ask for three summaries at once.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(volume), MAX(close)
FROM prices;
```
screens.question: How many rows does this query return?

options.why: You expected one result per input row. Each of these functions folds all five rows into one value.
You gave each function its own row. They sit side by side, as the columns of one row.

hints.text: How many values did `MAX(close)` give on its own?
`COUNT(*)` counts the rows: one number.
Three single values side by side make one row with three columns.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each function on its own returns one value.

byKey.five: You expected one result per day. Each function folds the five days into one value.

explain.text: `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` are **aggregate functions**. Each folds a column into a single value, so the result is one row: `(5, 10600000, 120.25)`.

canvas.caption: five rows in, one row out

screens.title: The average close
screens.question: What does this return? Give pounds to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Add the five closes first.
The closes sum to £595.15.
Divide £595.15 by the 5 rows.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the five closes, then divide by how many there are.

byKey.sum: You added the closes but did not divide. `AVG` divides the sum by the count.
byKey.median: You took the middle close when sorted. `AVG` is the mean, not the median.
byKey.four: You divided by 4. There are five closes in the table.

explain.text: The closes sum to £595.15 over 5 rows, so `AVG(close)` is £119.03. It reads one column and returns one value, like `MAX`.

screens.title: Write it
screens.prose: The starter builds the same `prices` table in memory. Your `query()` returns the SQL as a string, and the tests run it. `ROUND(x, 2)` rounds `x` to two decimals.
screens.question: Return one row: the number of days, the total volume, and the average close rounded to 2 decimal places.

widget.starter:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE prices(date TEXT, ticker TEXT, close REAL, volume INTEGER)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO prices VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    ("2024-03-11", "AZN", 118.40, 2100000),
    ("2024-03-12", "AZN", 119.10, 1900000),
    ("2024-03-13", "AZN", 117.60, 2600000),
    ("2024-03-14", "AZN", 120.25, 2300000),
    ("2024-03-15", "AZN", 119.80, 1700000),
])


def query():
    return """
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM prices
"""
widget.solution:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE prices(date TEXT, ticker TEXT, close REAL, volume INTEGER)")
db.executemany("INSERT INTO prices VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)", [
    ("2024-03-11", "AZN", 118.40, 2100000),
    ("2024-03-12", "AZN", 119.10, 1900000),
    ("2024-03-13", "AZN", 117.60, 2600000),
    ("2024-03-14", "AZN", 120.25, 2300000),
    ("2024-03-15", "AZN", 119.80, 1700000),
])


def query():
    return """
SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(volume), ROUND(AVG(close), 2)
FROM prices
"""

tests.setup: t2 = sqlite3.connect(":memory:"); t2.executescript("".join(db.iterdump())); t2.executescript("INSERT INTO prices VALUES ('2024-03-18', 'AZN', 121.20, 1800000);")
t3 = sqlite3.connect(":memory:"); t3.executescript("".join(db.iterdump())); t3.executescript("DELETE FROM prices WHERE date < '2024-03-13';")

widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests. Each runs your query and compares the rows from `fetchall()` exactly, so round in the query. Tests after the first add rows to a copy of the data.

hints.text: Put the three aggregates in one `SELECT`, separated by commas.
`ROUND(AVG(close), 2)` rounds the mean to two places.
`SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(volume), ROUND(AVG(close), 2) FROM prices`

feedback.correct: One row, three columns, and the average fixed to two places.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the examples and compare your row with the expected one.

byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[(5, 10600000, 119.03)]`. Check the order of your three columns.
byKey.test-2: Test 2 adds a sixth day. A typed-in number cannot follow it, but the aggregates can.

explain.text: Three aggregates in one `SELECT` give one row with three columns. `ROUND` fixes the float to two places, so the test can compare it exactly.

screens.title: Filter, then fold
screens.prose:
Add a filter.

```sql
SELECT SUM(volume)
FROM prices
WHERE close > 119;
```
screens.question: Tap every volume that this sum adds.

hints.text: Which days closed above £119?
Read the close column first.
Keep 12, 14 and 15 March, then tap their volumes.

feedback.correct: Three days closed above £119, so the sum is 5,900,000 shares.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the rows whose close is above £119.

byKey.all: You added every day. `WHERE` removes the rows with a close of £119 or less before `SUM` sees them.
byKey.r0c3: 11 March closed at £118.40, below £119, so `WHERE` drops that row.
byKey.r2c3: 13 March closed at £117.60, so `WHERE` drops that row.

explain.text: `WHERE` runs first and keeps three rows. `SUM` then adds only their volumes: 1,900,000 + 2,300,000 + 1,700,000 = 5,900,000.

canvas.caption: WHERE keeps 3 rows, then SUM adds them

screens.title: A missing close
screens.prose:
The data vendor sent nothing for 13 March, so that close is `NULL`.

```sql
SELECT AVG(close)
FROM prices;
```
screens.question: What does this return? Give pounds to 2 decimal places.

hints.text: Is a missing close the same as a close of £0?
Only four closes are known.
Add the four known closes, £477.55, and divide by 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide what `AVG` does with the row that has no close.

byKey.as-zero: You counted the missing close as £0 and divided by 5. `AVG` skips the `NULL`, so it divides by 4.
byKey.sum: You added the four closes but did not divide.

explain.text: `AVG` leaves the `NULL` row out entirely: £477.55 over 4 closes is £119.39. Treating it as £0 would drag the average down to £95.51. `COUNT(*)` still counts 5 rows, but `COUNT(close)` counts 4 values.

screens.title: The pattern
screens.prose:
Every aggregate reads the rows that survive `WHERE` and returns one value. Each skips `NULL`, except `COUNT(*)`, which counts rows.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(close), SUM(volume),
       ROUND(AVG(close), 2), MIN(close), MAX(close)
FROM prices
WHERE ...;
```
screens.question: On this table, what do `COUNT(*)` and `COUNT(close)` return?

options.why: You counted the `NULL` as a close. `COUNT(close)` counts only the values that are present.
`COUNT(*)` counts rows, whatever they hold. The row for 13 March is still a row.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. One counts rows; the other counts values.

explain.text: `COUNT(*)` counts the five rows. `COUNT(close)` skips the `NULL` and counts four.

screens.title: Why the average skipped a day
screens.prose:
We can write what `AVG` did, one line at a time, for a column $c$.

$$\begin{aligned} \text{AVG}(c) &= \frac{\text{sum of the values present}}{\text{number of values present}} && \text{NULLs are skipped} \\ &= \frac{\text{SUM}(c)}{\;?\;} && \text{SUM also skips NULLs} \end{aligned}$$
screens.question: Which denominator completes the second line?

options.why: That divides by every row, so the `NULL` acts as a £0 close. It gives the £95.51 answer.
Subtracting 1 fixes this table only, which has one `NULL`. A table with two would break it.

hints.text: The numerator only adds values that are present.
Which count also skips the `NULL`?
`COUNT(c)` counts the values present: 4 here.

feedback.correct: Both sides skip the `NULL`, so they match.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The denominator must skip the same rows as the numerator.

explain.text: `SUM(close)` adds the 4 values present, so it must be divided by the 4 that `COUNT(close)` counts. Here $c$ is the close column. £477.55 / 4 = £119.39, the value you found.

import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")

db.executemany("INSERT INTO trades VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", [

widget.how: Check runs 3 hidden tests. Each compares the rows from `fetchall()` exactly. Test 2 adds a fill on 12 March; test 3 adds one on another day.

hints.text: Filter to the day first, then fold.
`WHERE date = '2024-03-12'` keeps four fills.
`SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(qty), ROUND(SUM(qty * price), 2) FROM trades WHERE date = '2024-03-12'`

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the examples and compare your row with the expected one.

byKey.test-3: Test 3 adds a fill on 14 March. If it changed your answer, the `WHERE` line is missing or wrong.
byKey.test-1: Test 1 expects `[(4, 13700, 111750.0)]`. Check the filter and the order of the columns.

explain.text: `WHERE` keeps the four fills from 12 March, then each aggregate folds them. `SUM(qty * price)` multiplies inside each row before adding, so every fill counts at its own price.

ideas: An aggregate function folds a whole column into one value, so a query of aggregates returns one row.
`WHERE` runs first: only the rows it keeps reach `COUNT`, `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX`.
Every aggregate skips `NULL` except `COUNT(*)`, which counts rows; round averages with `ROUND(x, 2)`.

formula.name: Average with missing values
formula.note: Divide by the values present, not by `COUNT(*)`.

summary.trap: A `NULL` close is not £0: `AVG` leaves that row out instead of averaging in a zero.

quiz.prose:
On the AstraZeneca week, every close is below £121.

```sql
SELECT COUNT(*)
FROM prices
WHERE close > 200;
```
quiz.question: What comes back?

options.why: You expected an empty filter to give an empty result. An aggregate with no `GROUP BY` always returns one row.
`COUNT` of nothing is 0. It is `SUM`, `AVG`, `MIN` and `MAX` that give `NULL` when no rows reach them.

feedback.correct: No rows survive, and the count of nothing is 0.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think about what counting zero rows gives.

explain.text: No row passes `WHERE`, so `COUNT(*)` counts nothing and returns 0. A whole-table aggregate still returns exactly one row.

quiz.prose:
Same table, same impossible filter.

```sql
SELECT SUM(volume)
FROM prices
WHERE close > 200;
```
quiz.question: What comes back?

options.why: You expected an empty sum to be 0. SQL returns `NULL` when no rows reach `SUM`.
A whole-table aggregate always returns one row, even when no rows pass `WHERE`.

feedback.correct: With no values to add, `SUM` returns `NULL`.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. `SUM` and `COUNT` differ on an empty set.

explain.text: `SUM` over no rows is `NULL`, not 0, in SQL. `COALESCE(SUM(volume), 0)` turns it into 0 when a report needs a number.

quiz.prose: A table has 8 daily closes, and 3 of them are `NULL`. The known closes add up to £600.00.
quiz.question: What does `ROUND(AVG(close), 2)` return? Give pounds.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Decide how many closes `AVG` divides by.

byKey.all-rows: You divided by all 8 rows. `AVG` skips the 3 `NULL`s and divides by 5.

explain.text: `AVG(close)` is `SUM(close) / COUNT(close)`. Both skip the `NULL`s, so it is £600.00 / 5 = £120.00.

quiz.prose:
The AstraZeneca week has a mean close of £119.03.

```sql
SELECT ROUND(AVG(close), 1)
FROM prices;
```
quiz.question: What does SQLite return?

options.why: You kept two places. The second argument of `ROUND` is the number of decimals to keep: 1.
`ROUND(x, 1)` keeps one decimal, and SQLite returns a float, so it shows `119.0`.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the second argument of `ROUND`.

explain.text: `ROUND(119.03, 1)` keeps one decimal place, and the 3 in the second place rounds down. The result is the float `119.0`.
